newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans suffer world's worst rape rate.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans suffer world's worst rape rate.

text.p: South Africa has the world's worst rape rate, due partly to lenient attitudes, and police are considering a new crusade to fight it, officials said on Friday.

National police commissioner George Fivaz may declare rape "a priority crime", his office said, but in a country also plagued by murder, armed robbery, carjackings and other violent crime, resources are stretched.
Interpol's latest figures, for 1994, show one rape reported in South Africa for every 1,000 people, and local police said on Friday the figure had risen by over a tenth since then.
This is almost three times higher than the U.S. rate and 12 times higher than Germany's, both countries where anti-rape campaigners say women are far more likely to go to the police.

A stream of gruesome cases since the new year, and the alarming figures, have catapulted rape onto the national agenda, prompting Justice Minister Dullah Omar to urge courts early this week to mete out tougher punishments to those convicted.
Armed robbers gang-raped a pair of teenagers and a pair of young women at luxury homes in the "crime capital" Johannesburg, their screams heard by their parents and relatives tied up in other rooms.
In staid Pretoria, 45 minutes drive away, rapists have attacked numerous young students and two girls were abducted as they took a summer stroll in the botanical gardens, then raped.
Minors make up a third of South Africa's known rape victims.
Reported rapes -- one on average every 14 minutes -- are only the tip of the iceberg, say anti-rape campaigners.
Citing internal South African police calculations, they say only one rape is reported for every 20 to 35 committed.

Callers to radio phone-ins say rapists should be castrated, flogged or hanged, mirroring overwhelming national support for a return of the death penalty which President Nelson Mandela has ruled out. It was last carried out in 1989 and scrapped by the Constitutional Court in 1995.

People have applauded vigilantes or parents who, in rage or in despair at an overburdened justice system, take the law into their own hands -- such as a policeman who went to the cells and shot dead the suspected rapist of his six-year-old daughter.
The Safety and Security Ministry called on Friday for better policing, more sensitive courts and an education drive to change attitudes of people who look on rape too lightly.
It backed Omar's suggestion of special courts to deal with rape cases and to lessen the ordeal for victims in the hope that more will come forward.

"The theory is that a woman who reports the crime gets raped three times," said ministry spokesman Maxwell Mulaudzi. "Once when it happens, again when she has to report and explain it and a third time under cross-examination in court."

Victim support groups say some South Africans -- insensitive policemen among them -- still see most rape victims as women who "ask for it" by their dress or behaviour, and underestimate the crime's devastating effects.
Counsellors list the long-term effects: eating problems, mood swings, nightmares, frequent washing, lack of trust, fear of being alone, and relationship and sex problems.

Some victims in rough townships say rape is almost inevitable for young women growing up there. The community has partly learned to live with it and few victims bother to report the attacks, often by people they know.
